assumptions._note: GAM Research forecast drivers for Berger Paints India (consolidated, ₹ crore). Berger reports one segment ('Paints and Coatings'), so the engine runs on a single revenue-growth path and an EBITDA-margin path; the business-line build (decorative vs industrial, sized on the company's FY26 split of 82% / 18%) sits in `businessLines` and the authoring script checks that it sums to model revenue. Other income = treasury yield × opening net cash (Screener basis) + non-treasury income (share of profit of the two 49% JVs plus income the Screener cash line does not explain). Valued on P/E, as the street does.
assumptions._revenueWhy: FY27 +12%: Q1 +12.0% (standalone volume +8.4%, price/mix ~5%; decorative value ~13.5%). Management guides to double-digit growth, Q2 'slightly ahead' of Q1 (volume 7.5-8%, price 7.5-8.5%) as industrial price rises flow in. H2 still carries the Mar-Jun 2026 price rises but faces possible post-Diwali cuts if crude stays lower (Brent fell ~15% in June) and bigger dealer rebates; we assume H2 ~+11%. FY28 +9%: price laps and part is given back; volume ~9% (FY26 standalone quarters ran 6-12%). FY29 +10%: volume ~9% plus ~1% mix. Business lines: decorative +12.5% / +9% / +10%, industrial +10% / +9% / +10%.

businessLines._why: Company split: industrial 18% of consolidated sales in FY26 (AR FY26 MD message), decorative the rest (~80% per CRISIL). Subsidiaries (Bolix, STP, Nepal) are inside these shares as the company reports them. FY27 decorative +12.5%: Q1 value ~13.5% and Q2 price impact 7.5-8.5% on ~8% volume, H2 slower. Industrial +10%: price rises came late in Q1 ('protracted battle'), catch up from Q2; protective helped by government capex; automotive by GST cuts.

assumptions._marginWhy: Consolidated EBITDA margin 16.1% (FY25), 15.4% (FY26), 16.9% in Q1FY27 (16.5% a year earlier). Guided range 15-17% (management, every quarter); CRISIL expects 15-17%. FY27 16.0%: Q2 is seasonally weak (12.5% in Q2FY26) but should be up year on year as industrial price rises flow in; H2 risks are dealer rebates and price give-backs. FY28 16.0%, FY29 16.2%: cheaper inputs offset by price give-backs and competitive spends; the new plants add fixed cost before they fill. Each 1pp of margin is ~₹145 cr of EBITDA (~7% of FY28E EPS).
assumptions._capexWhy: FY27 guidance ₹600-800 cr (5-Aug-2026); Panagarh (West Bengal) and Khordha (Odisha) plants cost ₹1,800-2,000 cr together, Panagarh to start at the end of FY27; CRISIL (28-Aug-2026) expects ~₹1,000 cr a year over the next few years. FY24-26 capex ₹275 / 429 / 518 cr (Screener).
assumptions._depWhy: FY26 depreciation ₹392 cr = 7.5% of average gross block (₹5,251 cr); Q1FY27 ₹103 cr (₹412 cr annualised). The engine depreciates capex at once while the new plants sit in CWIP until commissioned, so we use 7.0%: FY27E ≈ ₹410 cr, in line with the Q1 run-rate, rising as the plants start.
assumptions._treasuryWhy: 7% on opening net cash on Screener's basis (cash + investments - borrowings: Rs 859 cr at Mar-26), i.e. ~Rs 60 cr in FY27E, close to FY26 treasury income of Rs 61.8 cr (bank-deposit interest Rs 17.8 cr + mutual-fund gains Rs 44.0 cr, AR FY26 note 36). The company reports higher net cash (Rs 1,198 cr at Mar-26, Rs 1,424 cr at Jun-26): cash Rs 305 cr plus liquid mutual funds Rs 954 cr (AR note 54) less a little bank debt, whereas Screener deducts all borrowings including lease liabilities and adds the equity-accounted JV stakes. Using the company figure would add ~Rs 24 cr of income in FY27E (~1% of EPS); we stay on the Screener basis, which the model balance sheet uses.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Non-treasury other income, built only from sourced parts. (1) Share of profit of the two 49% JVs (Berger Nippon Paint Automotive, Berger Becker): Rs 35 cr (FY25), Rs 51 cr (FY26, +46%), Rs 11.8 cr in Q1FY27 (+5%); management says both JVs grew strongly and passenger-car demand is buoyant after the GST cut, so we take Rs 55 / 60 / 65 cr (~8% a year, in line with industrial revenue). (2) Recurring non-treasury items in consolidated other income (AR FY26 note 36): interest on non-bank items Rs 4.2 cr, discount income Rs 7.2 cr, arrangement fees Rs 1.8 cr, gains on early lease terminations Rs 5.4 cr and miscellaneous income Rs 15.0 cr = Rs 33.5 cr in FY26 (Rs 30.4 cr in FY25); held at Rs 33 cr. One-offs (insurance claims, gains on asset sales, balances written back, the FY25 fair-value gain on Surefire: Rs 11.4 cr in FY26, Rs 21.3 cr in FY25) are left out. FY27E total other income (incl. treasury) ~Rs 148 cr vs Rs 152 cr in the twelve months to Jun-26 on Screener (which also nets the Labour Code charge and the insurance recovery).
assumptions._interestWhy: FY26 ₹58 cr, Q1FY27 ₹12.5 cr; no long-term debt; plants funded from cash (CRISIL).
assumptions._taxWhy: FY26 ₹360 cr on ₹1,488 cr PBT (24.2%); Q1FY27 25.4% (₹137.6 cr on ₹542.6 cr). The engine taxes JV income (already post-tax) too, so 25% slightly understates EPS (~₹15 cr).
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend ₹4.00 a share (₹466 cr, 41% of profit); FY25 ₹3.50 (35%). No buyback planned (MD, Feb-2026); capex absorbs cash.

dcf._betaWhy: Net cash, consumer-facing franchise with a dominant domestic business; below-market sensitivity (Ke 11.3%), same as the house treatment of Pidilite and Asian Paints-type compounders.
dcf._tgWhy: India's nominal GDP grows ~10%; per-capita paint use is 4.1 kg vs 13-15 kg globally, so the category can grow above GDP for long, but with more competitors. Top of the house 5-6% range: 6%.
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~10% to 8% by year 15: volume growth of 8-10% a year has been steady, pricing is no longer a lever with Birla Opus and JSW in the market.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: Holds at 16%, the middle of management's 15-17% range.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Capex falls from ~5.6% of revenue (plant build) to 3.5%, near the FY24-26 average of ~3.7%.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Price rises stick through FY28 while inputs ease, Birla Opus and JSW Dulux stay rational (Investec's 'peak intensity is over'), volume runs at 10-11% on new stores and tinting machines, and margin sits at the top of the 15-17% range.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: Prices are cut after Diwali faster than inputs fall, the challengers step up dealer schemes again and Berger loses share (as in 9MFY26), volume slows to 5-6% and margin drops to the bottom of the range.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: How the street values Berger: P/E on FY28E or Jun-28E EPS (Nomura 50x FY28E, Monarch Networth 48x FY28E, Equirus 46x Jun-28E; ICICI Securities' DCF target equals ~40x FY28E). 37x = Berger's 52x median one-year-forward P/E since Apr-2021 (no trough years excluded: forward EPS never fell below half its prior three-year peak), cut by the ~30% median de-rating of four paint and adhesive peers (Asian Paints, Kansai Nerolac, Pidilite, Indigo) versus their five-year median P/E by 30-Sep-2026 (36.6x, rounded). No further growth adjustment: our FY27-29E EPS growth (~10% a year after the price-led FY27 jump) is in line with FY21-26 (~9%). Bull 45x (its 25th-percentile forward P/E since 2021); bear 29x (the median cut by the worst peer de-rating, Kansai Nerolac's 44%: Berger priced as a share loser).

methods.name: EV/EBITDA
methods.why: Counts net cash at face value. 20x Sep-28E EBITDA = Berger's 36x median trailing EV/EBITDA since Apr-2021, less the same ~30% sector de-rating (25.5x trailing), restated for Sep-28E EBITDA being ~28% above the twelve months to Jun-26 (≈20x). Bull 24x, bear 16x scale with the P/E multiples.

methods.name: DCF
methods.why: Tests whether cash flows support the price: 15-year FCFF, Ke 11.3%, terminal growth 6%, plus net cash.

cover.headline: A strong No.2 that new rivals have made cheaper to fight: volumes keep growing, pricing power has not come back, and the stock is fairly priced
cover.lead: Berger is India's second-largest paint company (~20% of listed players' sales), with 64,000+ dealers, No.1 in protective coatings and net cash. Its problem since 2024 is not volume (standalone volume grew 4-12% a quarter) but value: Grasim's Birla Opus pushed dealer schemes up and prices down, JSW took over Dulux in Dec-2025, and Berger's revenue grew only 3% a year in FY25-26. The 2026 crude spike reversed that for now: Q1FY27 revenue rose 12% (volume +8.4%, price ~5%) and PAT 29%. The street values Berger on **P/E (46-50x FY28E EPS)**. We forecast EPS of ₹11.7 (FY27E), ₹12.7 (FY28E) and ₹14.1 (FY29E). Applying **37x to Sep-28E EPS of ₹13.4** gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with HOLD.** Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹433, DCF ₹263. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: In the eight quarters to Q4FY26 standalone volume grew 4-12% but value only −0.4% to +6.7%: cheaper products (putty, textures, tile adhesives), economy-emulsion price cuts and heavier dealer schemes. Q1FY27's 12.7% value growth is the industry's crude-led price rise (list prices +12-13%, ~5% realised), not new pricing power.

Birla Opus sold ₹1,661 cr of paint in Q1FY27 (+64%), half Berger's standalone quarter, and calls itself the No.3 organised decorative player. Berger's share stopped rising at ~20% and the MD admitted a small loss in 9MFY26, "mostly to Birla". The challenger has raised its list prices, but rebates and "10% free material" continue.

arguments.h: FY27 is a good year; FY28 is the test
arguments.p: We model EPS +{{F.epsGrowth.0|pct}} in FY27E (price, operating leverage, a low FY26 base hit by one-offs), then +{{F.epsGrowth.1|pct}} and +{{F.epsGrowth.2|pct}} as price laps and part is given back. EBITDA margin {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}}, inside the 15-17% band Berger has lived in for a decade.

At ₹455 the stock trades at 39.0x our FY27E and 35.9x FY28E EPS. Its 52x median forward P/E since 2021, cut by the ~30% de-rating of paint and adhesive peers, gives 37x and {{dcf.tp|inr}}. The DCF (₹263) shows the price still assumes long, high growth.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): realised price (guided 7.5-8.5%), volume (guided 7.5-8%) and whether the margin rose year on year as promised.
Post-Diwali pricing: if crude stays lower, a price cut or bigger dealer rebates would hit FY28 value growth; past cuts came 3-4 months after inputs fell.
Birla Opus and JSW Dulux: Grasim's quarterly paint revenue, dealer schemes, painter incentives.
Panagarh plant start (end of FY27) and the capex run-rate (₹600-800 cr guided for FY27).
East India demand: West Bengal (a large market for Berger) after the change of government; North-East floods.

sections.title: India's No.2 paint maker: four-fifths decorative, one-fifth industrial

blocks.p: Berger makes paints and coatings. **Decorative** paints (about 82% of FY26 consolidated sales) go on homes and buildings: interior and exterior emulsions, enamels, distempers, putty and primers, wood coatings, and a fast-growing range of construction chemicals and waterproofing (Home Shield, Roof Kool & Seal, Dampshield) and tile adhesives. They are sold through 64,475 dealers, most of whom tint paint to order on Berger's machines, and applied by contract painters, who influence what the homeowner buys. **Industrial** coatings (18%) are sold to companies: protective coatings for bridges, refineries, pipelines and rail (Berger is No.1 in India), automotive coatings (directly and through a 49% joint venture with Nippon Paint), general industrial and powder coatings, and coil coatings through a 49% joint venture with Becker. Subsidiaries add ₹1,460 cr of revenue (net of eliminations): Bolix in Poland (external insulation systems), BJN in Nepal (decorative paints), STP (construction chemicals) and smaller Indian units.

sections.title: A growing market that turned from a cosy oligopoly into a capacity race

blocks.p: Indian paint demand grows with housing, repainting, rising incomes and the shift from lime wash and unbranded paint to branded emulsions. Use per person is low (about 4.1 kg against a global average of 13-15 kg) and the unorganised sector is still nearly a quarter of the market. For two decades the organised market was a stable oligopoly led by Asian Paints, with Berger, Kansai Nerolac and Akzo Nobel (Dulux) behind; prices rose with inputs and rarely fell much. That changed in 2024, when Grasim launched Birla Opus with large new plants and aggressive dealer terms, and again in Dec-2025, when JSW Paints took control of Akzo Nobel India. Industry value growth fell close to zero in FY25-26 while volumes kept growing.

The cost side is crude oil. Petroleum derivatives (solvents, monomers for emulsions, resins) are 55-60% of raw materials and titanium dioxide is the other big input. When the West Asia conflict lifted crude in early 2026, the industry raised prices 14-16% in stages between March and June, Birla Opus included. That is why Q1FY27 growth jumped for every listed player. The question for FY28 is how much of it stays when inputs ease.

sections.title: Birla Opus and JSW: Berger is holding volume share, but paying for it

blocks.p: Grasim launched Birla Opus in 2024 with large new plants and generous dealer terms; by Q1FY27 it was selling ₹1,661 cr of paint a quarter (+64% year on year), about half of Berger India's quarterly sales, and calls itself the No.3 organised decorative player. Berger's own numbers show what that did. Volume kept growing (standalone 4-12% a quarter) and its share of the five listed players' sales rose to a company-estimated 20.3% in FY25 and 21.2% in Q1FY26, because Asian Paints lost more. But value growth collapsed to −0.4% to +6.7%, and in Feb-2026 the MD conceded a small loss: share "was at 19.5, 19.6, it would have probably gone down to 19.4", gone "mostly to Birla". In Aug-2026 he said Berger had regained "a little bit" in Q1FY27.

blocks.p: Partly. Berger's gross margin did not fall: the standalone figure was 41.2% and 42.3% in Q3-Q4FY26, the best in three years, helped by cheaper inputs, mix and the end of the anti-dumping duty on titanium dioxide. The money went below the gross line. In FY26 consolidated other expenses (which include advertising and selling costs) rose to 19.4% of revenue from 18.3%, and staff costs to 7.7% from 7.1%, so EBITDA margin fell from 16.1% to 15.4% even as gross margin rose. Management keeps guiding to 15-17% and Q1FY27 came in at 16.9%. Our read: the band has not moved, but Berger now needs a good gross margin just to stay in the middle of it, and any price give-back in FY28 lands on a cost base that has been raised for good.

bullets: **What the challenger is doing now (MD, 5-Aug-2026):** its dealer price list was ~5% below Berger's and has been raised to match; rebates to bigger dealers went up; "10% free material continues in most of the packs"; painter spends normalised. Intensity "reduced, but it still remains at an elevated level".
**Other entrants:** smaller and foreign players together cut industry growth by "1-1 and a half percent" (MD, Feb-2026); Pidilite's Haisha is entering East India, Berger's home market.

**Berger's response:** 11,100+ dealers added and 10,000+ tinting machines in FY26, 700 new stores, a corporate-brand campaign, new products (Kolor Plus, Roof Kool & Seal, Dampshield), and ad spend "on par" with its share while the challenger spends far above its share (MD).

**The bull case on competition:** Investec (May-2026) thinks "peak competitive intensity may be over" and sees Opus's further gains at ~1.5-2%; ICICI Securities notes Birla Opus raised prices more than peers in 2026.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** Berger is not losing the volume war; three-year revenue growth of 4% a year beat Asian Paints' 1% and Kansai's 2%. It has lost the pricing it used to enjoy, and it now spends more on dealers and brand to stand still. The 2026 price rises were an industry event caused by crude, not proof that discipline is back. We assume the 15-17% margin band holds, but at {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} in FY28E, not the top of it.

bullets: **What it is.** Paints, putty, wood coatings and construction chemicals for homes and buildings: ~₹9,742 cr in FY26 on the company's 82/18 split (CRISIL: ~80%). FY26 decorative volume +7.7%, value +3% (consolidated).

Management's own description: "volume growth happens to be there, but the value growth is relatively muted".

**Q1FY27.** Decorative value ~13.5% (highest in 12 quarters) and operating profit ~+20%, on calibrated price rises effective for part of the quarter, exterior emulsions and Kolor Plus. Some dealer stocking ahead of price rises ("there has been some amount of stocking up").

**Where it is strong.** A clear leader in the North-East and strong in East India (West Bengal is over 10% of revenue, per Equirus); under-indexed in the South and West, where most new tinting machines and the corporate-brand campaign are aimed. Project (builder) sales grow 1-2pp faster than retail.

**Competition.** The challenger's dealer price list was ~5% below Berger's and has been equalised; rebates to big dealers and 10% free material in most packs continue; painter incentives have normalised (MD, Aug-2026).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** decorative volume growth of 8-10% looks durable: more dealers, tinting machines and stores, construction chemicals, and a low base in many states. Value growth is the industry's to decide. blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** in decorative paints Berger has scale, a dense dealer and tinting network and a known brand, but not a wide moat. The last two years proved it: a new entrant with money built a No.3 position in about two years, and Berger had to cut prices in economy products and spend more to keep its share. The moat protects **volume share**, not **price**. The one place it is genuinely hard to dislodge is industrial (No.1 in protective coatings, JVs with Nippon Paint and Becker), and that is under a fifth of sales. Net: a well-run No.2 in an industry that has become more competitive for good; it does not deserve the premium multiple it carried in 2021.

sections.title: Ten years: revenue up 2.8x, but the last three years added only 4% a year

blocks.p: Berger's revenue grew from ₹4,223 cr in FY16 to ₹11,880 cr in FY26, about 11% a year, and net profit from ₹371 cr to ₹1,128 cr, also about 11-12% a year. The decade splits in two. Up to FY23 growth was strong: revenue jumped 29% in FY22 and 21% in FY23 as demand came back after Covid and the industry raised prices to pass on raw-material inflation. Since then revenue grew only 6%, 3% and 3% (FY24-26), even though volumes grew 7-9% a year: prices were cut in economy emulsions, the mix moved to cheaper products (putty, textures, tile adhesives), and new competitors (Birla Opus from 2024) pushed dealer schemes up. Profit followed: up 36% in FY24 when input costs fell, then flat in FY25 and down 5% in FY26 (including a ₹53 cr Labour Code charge).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** Berger is a steady compounder of volume (high single digits most years), but in paints the value line is set by the industry's pricing. When raw materials spike, everyone raises prices and revenue jumps (FY22-23, Q1FY27); when they fall or a new entrant buys share, prices drift down and revenue lags volume (FY24-26). bullets: **Cash backs profit.** Operating cash flow was 137% of net profit in FY26, 107% in FY25 and 136% in FY24; over FY15-26 cash from operations (₹9,899 cr) exceeded net profit (₹8,615 cr). FY22 (68%) was the exception, when inventory was built as input prices rose.

**One-offs are small and explained.** FY26: a ₹53.3 cr Labour Code charge (Q3) and a ₹36.8 cr warehouse fire (Q1) offset by an insurance claim receivable (Q4). Adding back the Labour Code charge, FY26 profit was roughly ₹1,170 cr, about flat on FY25.

**Other income is modest.** Screener's other income (₹104 cr in FY26, 7% of pre-tax profit) is the company's other income (₹106.7 cr: treasury ₹61.8 cr, recurring items such as discounts and miscellaneous income ₹33.5 cr, one-offs ₹11.4 cr; AR note 36) plus the share of JV profit (₹51 cr) less the ₹53.3 cr exceptional charge.
**Revenue is net of dealer schemes.** Rebates, discounts and free material are deducted from revenue; rising schemes show up as weaker value growth, which is what happened in FY25-26.

**Disclosure.** One reported segment; decorative vs industrial only as growth rates and an annual share; volume growth every quarter but no tonnage or realisation; market-share figures on a changing basket (21.2% in a company chart, "~20%" and "19.4%" elsewhere).
**Auditor change.** B S R & Co. LLP replaced S. R. Batliboi & Co. LLP from the 2025 AGM at the end of its term; FY26 opinion unqualified.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Strong cash conversion, small and explained one-offs, a simple balance sheet and a Big-Four auditor. The weaknesses are disclosure (no segment margins) and the dependence of reported revenue on scheme accounting in a price war.

assumptions._note: GAM Research forecast drivers for Berger Paints India (consolidated, ₹ crore). Berger reports one segment ('Paints and Coatings'), so the engine runs on a single revenue-growth path and an EBITDA-margin path; the business-line build (decorative vs industrial, sized on the company's FY26 split of 82% / 18%) sits in `businessLines` and the authoring script checks that it sums to model revenue. Other income = treasury yield × opening net cash (Screener basis) + non-treasury income (share of profit of the two 49% JVs plus income the Screener cash line does not explain). Valued on P/E, as the street does.
assumptions._revenueWhy: FY27 +12%: Q1 +12.0% (standalone volume +8.4%, price/mix ~5%; decorative value ~13.5%). Management guides to double-digit growth, Q2 'slightly ahead' of Q1 (volume 7.5-8%, price 7.5-8.5%) as industrial price rises flow in. H2 still carries the Mar-Jun 2026 price rises but faces possible post-Diwali cuts if crude stays lower (Brent fell ~15% in June) and bigger dealer rebates; we assume H2 ~+11%. FY28 +9%: price laps and part is given back; volume ~9% (FY26 standalone quarters ran 6-12%). FY29 +10%: volume ~9% plus ~1% mix. Business lines: decorative +12.5% / +9% / +10%, industrial +10% / +9% / +10%.

businessLines._why: Company split: industrial 18% of consolidated sales in FY26 (AR FY26 MD message), decorative the rest (~80% per CRISIL). Subsidiaries (Bolix, STP, Nepal) are inside these shares as the company reports them. FY27 decorative +12.5%: Q1 value ~13.5% and Q2 price impact 7.5-8.5% on ~8% volume, H2 slower. Industrial +10%: price rises came late in Q1 ('protracted battle'), catch up from Q2; protective helped by government capex; automotive by GST cuts.

assumptions._marginWhy: Consolidated EBITDA margin 16.1% (FY25), 15.4% (FY26), 16.9% in Q1FY27 (16.5% a year earlier). Guided range 15-17% (management, every quarter); CRISIL expects 15-17%. FY27 16.0%: Q2 is seasonally weak (12.5% in Q2FY26) but should be up year on year as industrial price rises flow in; H2 risks are dealer rebates and price give-backs. FY28 16.0%, FY29 16.2%: cheaper inputs offset by price give-backs and competitive spends; the new plants add fixed cost before they fill. Each 1pp of margin is ~₹145 cr of EBITDA (~7% of FY28E EPS).
assumptions._capexWhy: FY27 guidance ₹600-800 cr (5-Aug-2026); Panagarh (West Bengal) and Khordha (Odisha) plants cost ₹1,800-2,000 cr together, Panagarh to start at the end of FY27; CRISIL (28-Aug-2026) expects ~₹1,000 cr a year over the next few years. FY24-26 capex ₹275 / 429 / 518 cr (Screener).
assumptions._depWhy: FY26 depreciation ₹392 cr = 7.5% of average gross block (₹5,251 cr); Q1FY27 ₹103 cr (₹412 cr annualised). The engine depreciates capex at once while the new plants sit in CWIP until commissioned, so we use 7.0%: FY27E ≈ ₹410 cr, in line with the Q1 run-rate, rising as the plants start.
assumptions._treasuryWhy: 7% on opening net cash on Screener's basis (cash + investments - borrowings: Rs 859 cr at Mar-26), i.e. ~Rs 60 cr in FY27E, close to FY26 treasury income of Rs 61.8 cr (bank-deposit interest Rs 17.8 cr + mutual-fund gains Rs 44.0 cr, AR FY26 note 36). The company reports higher net cash (Rs 1,198 cr at Mar-26, Rs 1,424 cr at Jun-26): cash Rs 305 cr plus liquid mutual funds Rs 954 cr (AR note 54) less a little bank debt, whereas Screener deducts all borrowings including lease liabilities and adds the equity-accounted JV stakes. Using the company figure would add ~Rs 24 cr of income in FY27E (~1% of EPS); we stay on the Screener basis, which the model balance sheet uses.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Non-treasury other income, built only from sourced parts. (1) Share of profit of the two 49% JVs (Berger Nippon Paint Automotive, Berger Becker): Rs 35 cr (FY25), Rs 51 cr (FY26, +46%), Rs 11.8 cr in Q1FY27 (+5%); management says both JVs grew strongly and passenger-car demand is buoyant after the GST cut, so we take Rs 55 / 60 / 65 cr (~8% a year, in line with industrial revenue). (2) Recurring non-treasury items in consolidated other income (AR FY26 note 36): interest on non-bank items Rs 4.2 cr, discount income Rs 7.2 cr, arrangement fees Rs 1.8 cr, gains on early lease terminations Rs 5.4 cr and miscellaneous income Rs 15.0 cr = Rs 33.5 cr in FY26 (Rs 30.4 cr in FY25); held at Rs 33 cr. One-offs (insurance claims, gains on asset sales, balances written back, the FY25 fair-value gain on Surefire: Rs 11.4 cr in FY26, Rs 21.3 cr in FY25) are left out. FY27E total other income (incl. treasury) ~Rs 148 cr vs Rs 152 cr in the twelve months to Jun-26 on Screener (which also nets the Labour Code charge and the insurance recovery).
assumptions._interestWhy: FY26 ₹58 cr, Q1FY27 ₹12.5 cr; no long-term debt; plants funded from cash (CRISIL).
assumptions._taxWhy: FY26 ₹360 cr on ₹1,488 cr PBT (24.2%); Q1FY27 25.4% (₹137.6 cr on ₹542.6 cr). The engine taxes JV income (already post-tax) too, so 25% slightly understates EPS (~₹15 cr).
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend ₹4.00 a share (₹466 cr, 41% of profit); FY25 ₹3.50 (35%). No buyback planned (MD, Feb-2026); capex absorbs cash.

dcf._betaWhy: Net cash, consumer-facing franchise with a dominant domestic business; below-market sensitivity (Ke 11.3%), same as the house treatment of Pidilite and Asian Paints-type compounders.
dcf._tgWhy: India's nominal GDP grows ~10%; per-capita paint use is 4.1 kg vs 13-15 kg globally, so the category can grow above GDP for long, but with more competitors. Top of the house 5-6% range: 6%.
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~10% to 8% by year 15: volume growth of 8-10% a year has been steady, pricing is no longer a lever with Birla Opus and JSW in the market.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: Holds at 16%, the middle of management's 15-17% range.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Capex falls from ~5.6% of revenue (plant build) to 3.5%, near the FY24-26 average of ~3.7%.

bear.narrative: Prices are cut after Diwali faster than inputs fall, the challengers step up dealer schemes again and Berger loses share (as in 9MFY26), volume slows to 5-6% and margin drops to the bottom of the range.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: How the street values Berger: P/E on FY28E or Jun-28E EPS (Nomura 50x FY28E, Monarch Networth 48x FY28E, Equirus 46x Jun-28E; ICICI Securities' DCF target equals ~40x FY28E). 37x = Berger's 52x median one-year-forward P/E since Apr-2021 (no trough years excluded: forward EPS never fell below half its prior three-year peak), cut by the ~30% median de-rating of four paint and adhesive peers (Asian Paints, Kansai Nerolac, Pidilite, Indigo) versus their five-year median P/E by 30-Sep-2026 (36.6x, rounded). No further growth adjustment: our FY27-29E EPS growth (~10% a year after the price-led FY27 jump) is in line with FY21-26 (~9%). Bull 45x (its 25th-percentile forward P/E since 2021); bear 29x (the median cut by the worst peer de-rating, Kansai Nerolac's 44%: Berger priced as a share loser).

methods.name: EV/EBITDA
methods.why: Counts net cash at face value. 20x Sep-28E EBITDA = Berger's 36x median trailing EV/EBITDA since Apr-2021, less the same ~30% sector de-rating (25.5x trailing), restated for Sep-28E EBITDA being ~28% above the twelve months to Jun-26 (≈20x). Bull 24x, bear 16x scale with the P/E multiples.
